CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · JANUARY · FEBRUARY

Angle sum and congruence

Acute, obtuse or right-angled, as big as a football pitch or as small as a stamp: in every triangle the three angles add up to 180°. Here you learn how to prove something like that, not just measure it. Then you find out which three pieces of information fix a triangle uniquely, and you construct triangles with compasses and set square.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • tell a definition from a theorem and write theorems in if-then form
  • understand the angle sum theorem and write down its proof
  • know the congruence theorems SSS, SAS, ASA and SsA
  • construct triangles and decide whether there are no, one or several solutions
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How big is a straight angle?

$180^\circ$

How big is a right angle?

$90^\circ$

Two angles lie next to each other on a straight line. One is $50^\circ$. How big is the other?

$180^\circ - 50^\circ = 130^\circ$ (angles on a straight line)

A line crosses two parallels. One alternate angle is $70^\circ$. How big is the other?

Alternate angles at parallels are equal: $70^\circ$.

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1The angle sum theorem

The three torn-off corners always form a straight angle, that is $180^\circ$. But we have only tried a few triangles, and measuring is never quite exact. How do we know that it holds for every triangle? For that you need a proof.

A definition fixes what a word means: “A triangle with a right angle is called right-angled.” A definition cannot be proved, it is agreed.

A theorem is a statement that has to be deduced from what is already known. It is often written in if-then form. The part after “if” is the hypothesis, the part after “then” the conclusion. In a direct proof you go step by step from the hypothesis to the conclusion.

KEY POINT · ANGLE SUM THEOREM

Theorem: if $ABC$ is a triangle, then $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ$.

Proof: draw the parallel $p$ to $\overline{AB}$ through $C$. Next to $\gamma$ the angles $\alpha'$ and $\beta'$ appear at $p$.

(1) $\alpha' = \alpha$, because they are alternate angles at the parallels $p$ and $AB$.   (2) In the same way $\beta' = \beta$.

(3) $\alpha'$, $\gamma$ and $\beta'$ together form a straight angle: $\alpha' + \gamma + \beta' = 180^\circ$.

(4) Substituting (1) and (2) gives $\alpha + \gamma + \beta = 180^\circ$.   $\blacksquare$

What we use: alternate angles at parallels crossed by a line are equal, and a straight angle is $180^\circ$. You know both from Year 5.

The sign $\blacksquare$ at the end says: the proof is finished.

INTERACTIVE · THE ANGLE SUM

Drag the corners and watch the sum. Then switch to “Proof figure” and find $\alpha'$ and $\beta'$.

EXAMPLE 1 · CALCULATING THE THIRD ANGLE

In a triangle $\alpha = 48^\circ$ and $\beta = 67^\circ$. How big is $\gamma$?

By the angle sum theorem: $\gamma = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 67^\circ$.

$\gamma = 65^\circ$

EXAMPLE 2 · IN A QUADRILATERAL

What is the angle sum in a quadrilateral?

A diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles. Their angles together make up exactly the angles of the quadrilateral.

$2 \cdot 180^\circ = 360^\circ$

EXERCISES

Calculate the missing angle: a) $\alpha = 35^\circ$, $\beta = 85^\circ$   b) $\beta = 90^\circ$, $\gamma = 22^\circ$   c) $\alpha = \beta = 72^\circ$

a) $\gamma = 60^\circ$   b) $\alpha = 68^\circ$   c) $\gamma = 36^\circ$

Definition or theorem? a) “A triangle with three sides of equal length is called equilateral.”   b) “In an equilateral triangle every angle is $60^\circ$.” Write b) in if-then form.

a) definition   b) theorem: “If a triangle is equilateral, then each of its angles is $60^\circ$.”

Can a triangle have two right angles? Can it have two obtuse angles? Justify with the angle sum theorem.

No. Two right angles already make $180^\circ$, nothing is left for the third. Two obtuse angles together are more than $180^\circ$.

What is the angle sum in a pentagon? In a hexagon? Divide it into triangles starting from one corner.

Pentagon: 3 triangles, $540^\circ$. Hexagon: 4 triangles, $720^\circ$.

In a triangle extend the side $\overline{AB}$ beyond $B$. The angle between the extension and $\overline{BC}$ is called the exterior angle $\beta_1$. Prove: $\beta_1 = \alpha + \gamma$.

$\beta$ and $\beta_1$ are angles on a straight line.

Angles on a straight line: $\beta_1 = 180^\circ - \beta$. Angle sum theorem: $\alpha + \gamma = 180^\circ - \beta$. Both right-hand sides are equal, so $\beta_1 = \alpha + \gamma$. $\blacksquare$

TEST YOURSELF!

$\alpha = 48^\circ$, $\beta = 67^\circ$. How big is $\gamma$?

$180^\circ - 115^\circ = 65^\circ$

What is the angle sum in a quadrilateral?

$2 \cdot 180^\circ$

$\alpha = 50^\circ$, $\gamma = 60^\circ$. How big is the exterior angle at $B$?

$\alpha + \gamma = 110^\circ$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Congruence theorems

Whoever gives away three sides always gets the same triangle back. Whoever gives away only three angles does not: the triangles have the same shape but different sizes. So which three pieces are enough?

Two figures are called congruent if you can place them exactly on top of each other by translating, rotating or reflecting. Then they agree in all sides and all angles. The congruence theorems say which three pieces you only need to compare.

The letters tell you what is given: S for side, A for angle. In SAS the angle lies between the two sides, in ASA the side lies between the angles.

KEY POINT · CONGRUENCE THEOREMS

If two triangles agree …

SSS: … in all three sides,

SAS: … in two sides and the angle between them,

ASA: … in one side and the two angles next to it,

SsA: … in two sides and the angle opposite the longer side,

… then they are congruent.

ASA often works anyway: if you know two angles, the angle sum theorem gives you the third. So any side and two angles are enough.

Not a congruence theorem: AAA (only the shape is fixed) and ssA, when the angle lies opposite the shorter side.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH THREE PIECES?

Choose at the top what is given and move the sliders. When is there exactly one triangle?

EXAMPLE 3 · WHICH THEOREM?

Triangle 1: $a = 5$ cm, $b = 6$ cm, $\gamma = 40^\circ$. Triangle 2: $b = 6$ cm, $\gamma = 40^\circ$, $a = 5$ cm. Are they congruent?

The angle $\gamma$ lies between the sides $a$ and $b$. Both agree in these three pieces.

congruent by SAS

EXAMPLE 4 · ONLY ANGLES

Two triangles both have the angles $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $70^\circ$. Do they have to be congruent?

No. One triangle can look like an enlargement of the other. A length is missing.

not necessarily congruent

EXERCISES

By which congruence theorem is the triangle fixed uniquely? a) $a = 4$ cm, $b = 5$ cm, $c = 6$ cm   b) $c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 30^\circ$, $\beta = 80^\circ$   c) $b = 3$ cm, $c = 7$ cm, $\alpha = 110^\circ$

a) SSS   b) ASA   c) SAS ($\alpha$ lies between $b$ and $c$)

Write the congruence theorem ASA in if-then form. What is the hypothesis, what is the conclusion?

If two triangles agree in one side and the two angles next to it, then they are congruent. Hypothesis: the three pieces agree. Conclusion: the triangles are congruent.

A triangle has $c = 6$ cm, $\alpha = 40^\circ$ and $\gamma = 80^\circ$. Is it fixed uniquely? Which other angle do you know?

$\beta = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 80^\circ = 60^\circ$. Then $c$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are known: ASA. Yes, uniquely.

A square is divided into two triangles by a diagonal. Use a congruence theorem to justify that they are congruent.

Both triangles have two sides of the square as arms with a right angle between them: SAS. Or: the diagonal is shared, the two other sides are sides of the square: SSS.

In the widget try the case SsA with $c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 40^\circ$. For which lengths of $a$ are there two triangles, for which one, for which none?

From $a = 5$ cm on (so $a \geq c$) exactly one. For $a$ roughly between $3.2$ cm and $5$ cm two. Below that none. At about $3.2$ cm exactly the circle touches the arm: a right-angled triangle.

TEST YOURSELF!

$\alpha = 40^\circ$, $\gamma = 80^\circ$. How big is $\beta$?

$180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$

How many sides do you know in the congruence theorem ASA?

One side and two angles.

How many of the four congruence theorems SSS, SAS, ASA, SsA need at least two sides?

SSS, SAS and SsA: three.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Constructing triangles

The circle about $B$ with $4.5$ cm cuts the free arm at $A$ twice. So there are two different triangles with this information. A construction problem can therefore have no solution, exactly one or several.

Before you construct, you draw a sketch: a rough figure with the given pieces marked in colour. From it you make the plan. The construction description records every step. Only then do you draw accurately with compasses, ruler and set square.

At the end you ask: does a solution exist? Is it unique? The congruence theorems tell you when there is exactly one. With dynamic geometry software (DGS) such as GeoGebra you can change the information and watch the solution change.

KEY POINT · CONSTRUCTION PROBLEMS
  1. Draw a sketch, mark the given pieces.
  2. Write a construction description: what is drawn, in which order?
  3. Construct with compasses and set square, label the points.
  4. Check solvability: no, exactly one or several solutions? Justify.

Labelling: corners $A$, $B$, $C$ anticlockwise. The side $a$ lies opposite $A$, $b$ lies opposite $B$, $c$ lies opposite $C$.

No triangle is formed if the circles do not intersect or if the angles already add up to $180^\circ$ or more.

INTERACTIVE · NO, ONE OR TWO SOLUTIONS

In the case SsA you see the circle about $B$ and the free arm at $A$. Make $a$ smaller slowly.

EXAMPLE 5 · CONSTRUCTION DESCRIPTION SSS

Construct a triangle with $a = 5$ cm, $b = 4$ cm and $c = 6$ cm.

  1. Draw $\overline{AB}$ with $c = 6$ cm.
  2. Draw an arc about $A$ with $r = b = 4$ cm.
  3. Draw an arc about $B$ with $r = a = 5$ cm.
  4. The intersection above $\overline{AB}$ is $C$.
  5. Join $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $C$.

exactly one solution (SSS), because $4 + 5 > 6$.

EXAMPLE 6 · NO SOLUTION

Construct a triangle with $c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 100^\circ$ and $\beta = 85^\circ$.

$\alpha + \beta = 185^\circ$ is already more than $180^\circ$. The free arms move apart and never meet.

no solution

EXERCISES

Construct and write a construction description: a) $c = 7$ cm, $\alpha = 50^\circ$, $\beta = 45^\circ$   b) $b = 4$ cm, $c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 75^\circ$

a) draw $\overline{AB}$, mark $50^\circ$ at $A$ and $45^\circ$ at $B$, intersection $C$.   b) $\overline{AB} = 5$ cm, mark $75^\circ$ at $A$, measure $4$ cm along the arm: $C$.

Is there a triangle? a) $a = 3$ cm, $b = 4$ cm, $c = 8$ cm   b) $\alpha = 90^\circ$, $\beta = 90^\circ$, $c = 4$ cm   c) $a = b = c = 5$ cm

a) no, $3 + 4 < 8$: the circles do not intersect   b) no, the arms are parallel   c) yes, an equilateral triangle

Construct: $c = 6$ cm, $\alpha = 40^\circ$, $a = 4.5$ cm. Draw both solutions in different colours. Measure $\gamma$ in both.

The two triangles have roughly $\gamma \approx 59^\circ$ and $\gamma \approx 121^\circ$. Together the two $\gamma$-values make $180^\circ$.

A plot of land is triangular. Two sides are 40 m and 30 m long and enclose a right angle. Draw it to the scale 1 : 1000 (1 cm stands for 10 m) and measure the third side.

Drawing: 4 cm and 3 cm with a right angle. The third side measures 5 cm, so 50 m.

With dynamic geometry: construct a triangle with $c = 6$ cm and $\alpha = 30^\circ$ and put $C$ on the free arm. For which lengths $a$ are there two triangles? Explain what happens at $a = 3$ cm.

Two triangles for $3 \text{ cm} < a < 6$ cm. At $a = 3$ cm the circle only touches the arm: there is exactly one triangle, and it has a right angle at $C$.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many triangles are there with $a = 3$ cm, $b = 4$ cm, $c = 8$ cm?

None: $3 + 4 < 8$.

How many triangles are there with $c = 6$ cm, $\alpha = 40^\circ$, $a = 4.5$ cm?

Two, because $a$ is smaller than $c$ but long enough to reach the arm.

In the two solutions, how many degrees do the angles $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ make together?

$180^\circ$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

In a right-angled triangle one acute angle is $37^\circ$. How big is the other?

$180^\circ - 90^\circ - 37^\circ = 53^\circ$

The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$. How big are they?

Together these are 6 equal parts of $180^\circ$.

One part is $30^\circ$: so $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.

Connecting with chapter 1.2: in a triangle $\alpha$ is a third of $180^\circ$ and $\beta$ a quarter of $180^\circ$. What fraction of $180^\circ$ is left for $\gamma$?

$1 - \tfrac13 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac{5}{12}$, so $\gamma = \tfrac{5}{12} \cdot 180^\circ = 75^\circ$.

Find the mistake in the “proof”: “I drew and measured ten triangles. Each time I got $180^\circ$. So the angle sum theorem holds.”

Ten examples are not a proof for all triangles, and measuring is inexact. A proof has to hold for every triangle and may only use what is already known.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A proof more than 2000 years old

Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician Euclid wrote the “Elements” in Alexandria, a textbook in 13 books. It was used for more than 2000 years. In the first book, as Proposition 32, you find exactly our angle sum theorem, with a proof using parallels and alternate angles.

But the theorem is even older. The scholar Proclus wrote, some 700 years after Euclid, that the Pythagoreans, the followers of Pythagoras, had already proved it. Their proof drew the parallel through the top corner of the triangle, just as in our widget. Proclus relied on a lost history of geometry by Eudemus.

What is special: a proof holds for ever. What Euclid proved is still exactly as true today.

Sources: Euclid, Elements, Book I, Proposition 32. Proclus, Commentary on the First Book of Euclid’s Elements, on Proposition I.32 (citing Eudemus).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

DEFINITION AND THEOREM

definition: agreed · theorem: proved, often as “If …, then …”

hypothesis → conclusion

ANGLE SUM THEOREM

$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ$, proof with the parallel and alternate angles

$\alpha = 48^\circ$, $\beta = 67^\circ$ → $\gamma = 65^\circ$

CONGRUENCE THEOREMS

SSS, SAS, ASA, SsA (longer side opposite the angle)

AAA and ssA do not fix a triangle

CONSTRUCTING

sketch, description, construction, solvability

no, one or two solutions
